title: Global Development Dashboard
text:
This project uses the public Gapminder data set, which contains country-level observations across many years. The data file includes more than 1,700 rows of real country-year records, making it a proper observational data set rather than a static plan.
The chart below shows the core relationship in the data: countries with higher GDP per capita tend to have longer life expectancy.


                            
                                            





More than 1,700 observations across 142 countries
Coverage runs from 1952 to 2007
The pattern is strong: higher GDP per capita is associated with longer life expectancy
The project is now built around actual observations, not a generic diet plan

title: Exploration
text:
This page treats the data as a set of observations to be questioned and visualized rather than as a fixed narrative. We can look for patterns, compare groups, and test whether development trends appear consistently across countries and time.




                            
                                            


The general pattern is clear: as GDP per capita rises, life expectancy tends to rise as well. The relationship is not perfectly linear, but the overall direction is consistent across continents.





                            
                                            


This view highlights broad structural gains over time. Average life expectancy rises steadily for every continent, but not at the same rate, which suggests differences in development, health systems, and social conditions.

title: Story
text:
The strongest story in this data is not about one country or one year. It is about a broad pattern that repeats across many observations: people in countries with stronger economies tend to live longer, and the gap between low-income and high-income countries narrows as development proceeds.
This is exactly the kind of pattern we can test with real-world data. We are not relying on a fixed opinion or a training plan; we are observing how variables move together in the world itself.


                            
                                            





The dataset shows a consistent relationship between income and health outcomes.
The trend is strongest when viewed across many countries and multiple years.
By 2007, the high-income countries sit at both the top of GDP per capita and the top of life expectancy.
This kind of project is useful because it gives us a real answer rather than a static recommendation.

The project is now grounded in an actual observational data set, and the homepage and analysis tabs work together to make the evidence readable and explainable.
